messages.subject: items nested within items (mixedmirt?)
parts:
Hi Phil, 

I hope I could get some advice from you. 

I have a clinical survey data where a single item have two responses. There are 24 items in total. The former response (binary) influences the latter responses (polytomous) to some degree.  On top of that, the content of the items are theoretically distinct (i.e. two factors: doing things on your own, doing things with others).

For example, 
  1. Walk down the street on your own. (18 items - F1)
  2. Walk down the street with your friends. (9 items - F2)
The responses to these questions are the following:
  • Do you feel you could do this right now (Yes/No)
  • How anxious would you feel doing this? (0 - No distress, 5 - moderate distress, 10 - extremely distress). 

In some cases, someone might feel anxious doing it (Yes), and have moderate distress (5). In other cases someone might not feel anxious doing it (0), but, they may also have moderate distress (5). The general correlation is that someone who is anxious will also feel distress and vice versa, though the correlation is not 1. This tells me that there is some sort of individual differences at work. 

My question is how best should I model such data under the mirt framework? My instinct would be to try multi-level mirt using the mixedmirt(), but most examples are based on person grouping variable rather than item grouping variable. I read through this thread (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!newtopic/mirt-package/mirt-package/gN0JeJVHoQA) as well, but the grouping variable was on the persons side. I was hoping that you could give some advice on how best I can use the mixedmirt() framework to model this type of data.

Thanks!
Aiden

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: items nested within items (mixedmirt?)
parts:
Hi Aiden,

Thanks for the question. From my perspective I don't really see the need to treat the Yes/No and distress indicators (0, 5, 10) as measuring different constructs, in that they both seem to be related to an anxiety/distress factor (i.e., a high score on distress more likely indicates a No response, while a low score on distress more likely indicates a Yes; hence, this seems like it's measuring roughly the same thing to me). So in this case I'd be tempted just to treat the data as coming from a two-factor correlated structure model based on social vs individual anxiety, and treat the observations as all indications of anxiety. HTH.

Phil
